one_liner: Plain-C Cortex-M4 memcpy with doubleword and unaligned-word loops; 1.3-5.3x faster than the toolchain memcpy on 10 KB copies.
what_it_does: A single C file (memcpy_fast.c) exporting memcpy_fast(to, from, n) with memcpy's signature and return value, meant as a faster bulk copy on STM32-class Cortex-M4 parts. It is not a symbol-level replacement: callers must call memcpy_fast explicitly, and there is no memmove variant for overlapping buffers. The same file carries memcpy_test(), an STM32 Standard Peripheral Library timing routine that is compiled in by default (#define MEMCPY_TEST at the top of the file).
how_it_is_fast: Alignment dispatch: when source and destination have the same address mod 8 and n >= 16, it copies the 1-7 head bytes to reach 8-byte alignment and then runs a long long loop intended to compile to LDRD/STRD (8 bytes per load/store pair). Otherwise it copies 32-bit words through possibly misaligned long pointers, relying on Cortex-M4 hardware support for unaligned LDR/STR, then a halfword and a byte for the tail. Most of the headline gain comes from the baseline, which falls back to byte copies whenever the two pointers are not both 4-byte aligned; memcpy_fast never copies bytewise for n >= 4.
when_to_use: Cortex-M4 firmware whose libc memcpy shows the baseline's pattern (byte speed whenever either pointer is not 4-byte aligned) and copies kilobyte-sized buffers at arbitrary byte offsets, such as packet or frame buffers.
Bulk copies between buffers with the same misalignment (both at offset 1, 2, 3, 5, 6 or 7 mod 8): 121-122 us versus 640-641 us for 10 KB in the author's table, about 5.3x.
8-byte-aligned bulk copies where the toolchain memcpy only runs a word loop: 121 versus 213 us, 1.76x.
GPL-3.0-compatible projects that can take a 130-line C file, fix its includes and inspect the generated assembly.
when_not_to_use: Toolchains whose memcpy is already tuned for Armv7-M (aligns the pointers and uses unaligned or multiple loads): the published gaps are against a memcpy that byte-copies any pair not both 4-aligned, and no comparison against a tuned memcpy exists.
Small copies: only 10240-10247-byte copies were timed; the cost of the dispatch, head and tail code for short copies is not documented.
Overlapping buffers: no memmove semantics (the unaligned path copies from the top word down, the aligned path from the bottom up).

Cores or configurations that trap unaligned word accesses (the code comment states the unaligned-access assumption for Cortex-M4 only), and 64-bit targets, since pointers are cast to u32; it cannot be unit-tested on a 64-bit PC unchanged.
Permissively licensed or proprietary firmware: GPL-3.0.

integration.dependencies: types.h for the u8/u32 typedefs (not in the repository); memcpy_test() additionally needs the STM32 Standard Peripheral Library (RCC, TIM5), CMSIS __disable_irq/__enable_irq and printf unless MEMCPY_TEST is removed
integration.min_toolchain: C99 compiler targeting 32-bit Arm; the test uses GCC-style __attribute__((aligned(8))); the compiler, version and flags behind the published numbers are not documented
integration.platforms: 32-bit Arm Cortex-M4 (STM32) with unaligned LDR/STR allowed; not 64-bit targets
integration.thread_safety: The copy functions are stateless and reentrant; memcpy_test() disables interrupts while it runs.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — same signature and return value as memcpy, but a different symbol name, no overlap handling, Cortex-M4-class targets only, and the file does not compile as shipped outside the author's project

gotchas: Build-flag sensitive: memcpy_aligned8's forward `*dto++ = *dfrom++` loop is a plain copy loop, and GCC's -ftree-loop-distribute-patterns pass (enabled at -O3 in GCC 9 and at -O2 and higher from GCC 10, per the releases' invoke.texi; tree-loop-distribution.c emits memcpy or memmove calls for such loops) can replace it with a call to the library routine it is meant to beat. Build the file with -fno-tree-loop-distribute-patterns and check the disassembly for LDRD/STRD.

Relies on undefined behaviour: memcpy_unaligned4 dereferences misaligned long pointers and both paths access byte buffers through long and long long lvalues (strict aliasing). The commented-out forward loop is annotated 'LDM,STM not support unaligned access', i.e. the compiler merged the accesses into multiple-load instructions that fault on unaligned addresses; the shipped reverse-indexed loop avoids that only with the author's compiler, so another compiler or optimisation level can bring the UsageFault back.

Does not compile as shipped outside the author's project: memcpy_fast.c defines MEMCPY_TEST unconditionally (pulling in STM32 SPL timer calls), includes a types.h that is not in the repository, and memcpy_fast.h uses size_t without including <stddef.h>.

Benchmark harness: only memcpy_fast's output is checked (memcmp over the copied range, so a write past n would go unnoticed), each pair is timed once with a 1 us timer, and the 5.25-5.29x rows compare word copies against the baseline's byte copies for equally misaligned pointers, a case any alignment-aware memcpy handles at aligned speed.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Prefer mmemmove (AJ528), Cortex-M assembly with memmove semantics measured against newlib-nano, when buffers may overlap or when the instruction choice must not depend on compiler flags; pick memcpy_fast only when you want C source you can audit and rebuild for a Cortex-M4. The Arm siblings copies-and-fills, arm-mem and Arm Optimized Routines target Cortex-A class cores, not Cortex-M.
verified_claims_summary: On an unnamed STM32 Cortex-M4 (clock, compiler, flags and libc not stated), copying 10240-10247 bytes between 8-aligned static buffers at offsets 0-7, memcpy_fast took 121-268 us against 213-641 us for the toolchain memcpy (TIM5 at 1 us, interrupts off): 1.32-1.33x for (4,0) and (0,4), 1.75-1.76x for (0,0) and (4,4), 2.39-3.41x for mismatched alignments and 5.25-5.29x for equal non-8-aligned offsets. The baseline runs at byte speed (640 us) for every pair that is not both 4-aligned, including equal misalignments such as (1,1), so it never aligns pointers before copying words and the top ratios measure word copies against byte copies (derived from page data).
status_note: Abandoned: 11 commits on 12 and 25 August 2020, no issues or releases, 7 stars; GPL-3.0 and small enough to rewrite, but it needs a types.h, removal of the built-in STM32 test and a disassembly check of the copy loops before use.
